questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics has a small marketing team of four. Its compliance officer is compiling guidance on which uses of Claude are acceptable, because colleagues have started using it informally.
questions.stem: Which of the following uses is the MOST clearly appropriate for these colleagues?

options.text: Brainstorming campaign taglines and names for a new service launch.
Deciding which of three competing carrier contracts to sign, based on the trade-offs.
Writing performance improvement plans for named employees who have missed targets.
Generating customer testimonials from scratch for the launch pages.

questions.explanation: Appropriate uses are ones where Claude contributes **ideas, structure or drafts** and a person judges and owns the result. Brainstorming taglines fits that exactly. The other three fail for reasons that are about the *kind* of decision, not the quality of the model: signing a contract, managing someone's performance, and putting invented words in a customer's mouth all carry consequences and accountability that cannot be delegated to a suggestion.

whyWrong.B: Choosing a contract is a business decision with legal and financial consequences. Claude can lay out the trade-offs for a human to weigh, but the decision itself is not the tool's to make.
whyWrong.C: Performance management affects someone's career and pay, and it needs context about the individual that Claude does not have.
whyWrong.D: Invented testimonials attributed to real-looking customers are deceptive, however good the writing is.

questions.mindset: Good fits are drafting and ideation. Decisions about people, money and commitments stay with people.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Legal handles a commercial dispute. A partner has two weeks to file a defence and the client's engineering director has asked for a summary of the technical issues that might arise. The firm has no in-house engineering expertise.
questions.stem: The partner asks a clerk to have Claude analyse the technical documents, write a first draft of the technical section, and produce a summary she can check. The draft is well organised and confidently worded. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: File the draft after the partner reads it once, since the partner is responsible for the filing and the wording is sound.
Have an independent qualified engineer verify the technical claims before anything goes into the filed document.
Add a disclaimer at the end of the section saying the analysis was AI-assisted and should be checked.
Replace the draft with a shorter version that stays closer to the wording of the source documents, to reduce the risk of overstatement.

questions.explanation: Claude is good at *organising and explaining* material a client has supplied; it is not a qualified engineer and does not understand whether a claim about a system is actually true. A filed court document carries legal consequences, and nobody at the firm can check this. An **independent subject-matter expert** is the control that fits that risk — which is the general principle: match the verification to who bears the consequences, not to how good the output sounds.

whyWrong.A: A partner reading once is a formality, not a technical verification, and nobody in the firm has the expertise to spot a plausible-sounding error. Accountability sits with the partner but competence still has to exist somewhere.
whyWrong.C: A disclaimer does not correct a wrong technical claim, and a filed document carrying a disclaimer is not made safer by it.
whyWrong.D: Sticking closer to the source wording reduces how much is invented, but Claude can still misread a document, and it does not address the missing expertise.

questions.mindset: Match the check to who bears the consequence: if no one in the room can verify it, bring in someone who can.

questions.scenario: Ivybridge College receives about 4,000 applications for 900 places on its nursing degree. The admissions team uses Claude as a first-pass screener to summarise each application and recommend a band.
questions.stem: The team wants to keep the tool for the volume of reading involved. Which framing is MOST defensible?

options.text: Claude summarises each application against the published entry requirements so a human makes the banding decision, and bands are checked for consistency across applicants with similar profiles.
Claude ranks all applicants by predicted likelihood of succeeding, and the top 900 are offered places automatically.
Claude screens out applications that do not mention the required subject or grade anywhere in the text, because missing data is objective.
Claude bands every application, and the team reviews only the ones it bands lowest, since the top bands are the least contentious.

questions.explanation: This is a high-impact decision about people's access to education, so the tool should help a person **read** rather than make the call. A is the defensible version: summarise against published criteria, let the human decide, and check that applicants with similar records are treated similarly — because a consistent-looking output can still be consistently wrong. Fairness in this pipeline is demonstrated, not assumed.

whyWrong.B: Automating the offer on a model's prediction removes human accountability entirely and ranks people on an inference nobody can defend to an applicant.
whyWrong.C: Absence of a keyword is not absence of the qualification. Relevant evidence is often in a reference, a portfolio or a later part of the document, so keyword filtering systematically drops some applicants.
whyWrong.D: Inverting the review to look only at the bottom assumes the top band is reliable, which is exactly the assumption the earlier stage of a pipeline most needs testing.

questions.mindset: In high-stakes decisions about people, let the tool widen human reading and keep the judgement human — then check for consistency.

questions.scenario: Rookwood Energy has received an information request from a resident asking whether Claude drafts are used to prepare responses to planning objections, and whether any personal data about objectors is stored in Claude.
questions.stem: The communications officer has a list of answers the communications officer believes to be true, some of which nobody has confirmed. What is the MOST appropriate way to respond?

options.text: Answer the questions that can be verified from the service's own records and settings, and say clearly which questions need to be checked before a response is sent.
Use Claude to draft a helpful, complete response to the resident and have a manager approve it, to avoid delaying the reply.
Answer everything as accurately as possible from the officer's own understanding of the system, and correct it later if the resident points out an error.
Decline to answer anything about the tools and refer the resident to the published AI policy page, which does not cover the specific systems asked about.

questions.explanation: A formal request for information is answered from **records and verifiable facts**, not from recollection. A is the responsible shape: answer what can be evidenced, and be explicit about what still needs checking rather than filling the gap. That is the same discipline as verifying any other claim that matters — confident phrasing is not the same as accuracy.

whyWrong.B: Drafting first and checking later is the wrong order for a formal response. Claude has no knowledge of this system's configuration and will produce plausible answers to fill the shape of the question.
whyWrong.C: Correcting after the fact is worse: a formal answer containing errors damages credibility and may be relied on by the requester in the meantime.
whyWrong.D: A general policy page does not answer specific factual questions. Non-responsiveness is itself a problem in a formal information process.

questions.mindset: Answer factual challenges from records you can evidence; never fill the gap with a confident guess.

questions.scenario: Calder & Sons, a scaffolding contractor, keeps a Project on its approved scaffold for planning enquiries. Two surveyors have proposed uploading photographs of a client's site to it so Claude can help identify hazards.
questions.stem: A colleague points out that these photographs will show an identifiable person's face and a street address. Which TWO pieces of advice are MOST appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Get the client's written consent for the specific intended use before uploading anything, and be clear about what the tool is and how the material will be handled.
Remove identifying detail such as faces and house numbers from the images before they go into the Project.
Ask Claude to describe each photo without repeating any personal details, so the original can still be uploaded in full.
Upload them, then delete the photographs once Claude has finished analysing them, so the exposure is short.
Use the photographs but add an instruction to the Project telling Claude never to mention anything about the client's address.

questions.explanation: Two different obligations are in play. **Consent and transparency**: site photographs of a client's property are not the contractor's to upload on a whim, and the client is entitled to know the tool involved (A). **Data minimisation**: removing faces and house numbers before upload reduces what personal data is ever exposed (B) — the better place to act, because anything uploaded has already left the contractor's control.

whyWrong.C: Asking the model not to repeat details leaves the personal data in the Project. The exposure happens at upload; filtering afterwards does not undo it.
whyWrong.D: Deleting afterwards is not a safeguard — the material has already been processed and stored by a third-party service in the meantime.
whyWrong.E: An instruction is not a control. The address is still in the file the Project can read, and instructions are not guaranteed to hold.

questions.mindset: Minimise before you upload, and get consent for uses that are not plainly your own to make.

questions.scenario: Silverbrook Foods' customer-service team handles about 300 enquiries a day by email. A supervisor wants to use Claude to help with the highest-volume, lowest-risk category: customers asking where an order is.

options.text: Let Claude draft replies from the order status for delivery enquiries, with a person checking and sending, and start with a narrow set of questions where the answer is verifiable.
Let Claude send delivery responses automatically, since order status is factual and the risk of a wrong answer is low.
Allow Claude to handle all enquiries, escalating to a person only when it is not confident about the answer.
Have Claude answer complaints about damaged goods as well, using the order record and the returns policy.

questions.explanation: Narrow scope, factual source, human send: that is the shape responsible automation takes. Drafting from a system record keeps the **content** grounded, and the human check keeps the **commitment** with the company. Starting with delivery enquiries — where the answer is checkable — means the team learns where it fails before widening the scope.

whyWrong.B: A factual-sounding answer can still be wrong — a wrong delivery date creates a missed delivery and a complaint, and the customer has no way to know it came from an automated system.
whyWrong.C: Confidence is not a reliable signal of accuracy, so routing by it means the worst cases are the ones least likely to reach a person. Complaints also carry judgement, not just facts.
whyWrong.D: A damaged-goods complaint requires empathy and a decision about liability. Widening scope before the narrow case is reliable inverts the learning order.

questions.mindset: Automate narrowly, from a checkable source, with a person sending — then widen only once it holds.

questions.scenario: Marden & Vale's data team wants to analyse two years of customer complaint records to find recurring themes. The records contain names, addresses, order numbers and free-text descriptions.
questions.stem: The team proposes asking Claude to work directly from the raw export, on the basis that the analysis is internal and the data is already on company systems. What is the BEST assessment?

options.text: Internal use and existing company custody do not remove the exposure created by processing personal data in a third-party service, so the data still needs minimising before it goes in.
Because the data is already held by the company and never leaves its systems, uploading it is acceptable without further checks.
The analysis is fine, but the team should delete the export afterwards to limit how long the data is held.
The team should proceed, but should ask Claude to avoid quoting names verbatim in its summary.

questions.explanation: The question is not where the data came from but **where it is going**. Moving identifiable customer records into a third-party processing service changes the exposure, and the safest control is to send less: strip names, addresses and order numbers to codes or aggregates before uploading, keep the re-identification key locally, and let Claude work on themes. Minimising beats deleting afterwards, because the exposure happens on upload.

whyWrong.B: This confuses where data is stored now with where it is processed next. Upload is a new disclosure, and personal data is exactly what data-protection expectations are written around.
whyWrong.C: Deletion afterwards limits duration but not the processing itself. The exposure occurred when the file went in.
whyWrong.D: Suppressing names in the output does nothing about the identifiers in the input, which remain in the service and in the transcript.

questions.mindset: Judge data handling by where the data goes, and send the least identifying version that still answers the question.

questions.scenario: Halcyon Legal's client intake form asks whether a prospective client has ever been diagnosed with a mental health condition, because the firm's insurance requires it. The form's explanatory text was written before the firm's policy on sensitive data was tightened.
questions.stem: The intake team wants to use Claude to summarise these forms into a single view for the partner who reviews them. Which consideration is MOST important before they proceed?

options.text: Health information is among the most sensitive categories of personal data, so its handling needs an explicit basis, clear necessity, and controls on who can see the summary.
The main risk is that Claude might misstate the answers, so the summary needs a fact-check against each original form.
The risk is mainly about how long the data is kept, so the summary should be deleted after the partner has read it.
The risk is mainly about the wording of the consent text, so the form should be reworded before any summarisation is considered.

questions.explanation: Some categories of personal data carry extra weight because the consequences of mishandling are severe for the person, not just for the organisation. Health information is the clearest example. That shifts the question from "is the analysis useful" to "is there an explicit basis for this, is it genuinely necessary, and who can see the result" — a question for the firm's privacy lead, not one the team settles for itself.

whyWrong.B: Accuracy matters, but it is not the governing concern here. A perfectly accurate summary of health data still needs an appropriate basis for processing it.
whyWrong.C: Retention matters, but shortening the life of the data does not address whether it should be processed in this way at all.
whyWrong.D: Wording the consent more clearly is worthwhile, but the substantive question is the basis and necessity for processing this category of data — a review, not a copy-edit.

questions.mindset: The more sensitive the category, the higher the bar for basis, necessity and access — escalate before processing.

questions.scenario: Arikon Freight's AI policy says: 'Do not use Claude for decisions about hiring, promotion or dismissal. Use of company AI tools must be disclosed in any client-facing document that AI helped produce.'
questions.stem: A recruiter wants Claude to draft rejection emails for unsuccessful candidates, on the grounds that it would save hours and the emails would be reviewed before sending. What is the correct response?

options.text: Decline: the policy excludes decisions about hiring, and the ranking that produces the rejection list is such a decision, whether or not a person reads the email.
Proceed, since a human reads and sends every email, so the human is making the decision.
Proceed, but have Claude rank the candidates and draft the emails, and record the ranking so decisions can be audited.
Proceed, but add a line to each email offering the candidate a conversation about the outcome, so the process is more humane.

questions.explanation: The policy prohibits **decisions**, and the decision point is the ranking, not the wording. If Claude decides who is a stronger candidate and the human only rubber-stamps it, the decision is still the tool's. That is also why reading the output is not a safeguard: a person who is not given the criteria, the alternatives or the evidence has nothing to review. Where policy is clear, the answer is to follow it rather than look for a reading that permits the work.

whyWrong.B: Human involvement in sending is not human involvement in deciding. Review without the basis for a judgement is not oversight.
whyWrong.C: Auditability makes an excluded decision traceable, not permitted. Recording a prohibited use does not make it compliant.
whyWrong.D: A more considerate template addresses tone, not the underlying question of whether the tool should be selecting candidates at all.

questions.mindset: Find where the decision is actually made. A policy about decisions is not satisfied by a human pressing send.

questions.scenario: Torrington Water's customer-service manager proposes giving the whole service department access to a Project that contains the current tariff document, the outage procedure and ten years of complaint records.
questions.stem: She reasons that 'only internal staff' will use it. Which TWO assessments are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Internal-only access does not remove the sensitivity of the material, and the Project's membership should be set by who needs it rather than by who might need it.
Since no customer will ever see the Project, the complaint records can be uploaded without any further review.
The Project should be restricted to the named service-desk staff who actually need the complaint records, with everyone else given an alternative for the tariff and outage information.
Broad access is acceptable provided the instructions tell Claude not to reproduce personal details from the complaint records.
The complaint records should be reduced — names and contact details replaced with codes — before they go into the Project at all.

questions.explanation: **A** is right because 'internal' is not a sensitivity category: data sensitivity follows the subject of the data, not the audience, and wider membership means wider exposure if anything goes wrong. **C** is the control that follows from it — set membership by need, so the handful of people who genuinely need the records have them. Note what C is *not* saying: it doesn't claim the records are harmless, only that their exposure should be narrow.

whyWrong.B: Personal data about customers does not become harmless because the audience happens to be colleagues. The audience affects who needs access, not how sensitive the data is.
whyWrong.D: An instruction is not an access control, and it asks the model to police data it has already been given.
whyWrong.E: Reducing the records is a good practice in its own right, but on its own it leaves a large group able to read personal data that most of them have no reason to see. It complements A and C rather than replacing them.

questions.mindset: Access follows need, not department. "Only staff" is not a sensitivity category.

questions.scenario: Ivybridge College's estates team has been using Claude to draft tender documents and has produced 40 documents with no record of AI assistance on them. Two tenders are submitted to a public body.
questions.stem: The estates director asks for a recommendation. Which is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Add an AI-assistance statement to the outstanding documents, and check the two submitted tenders against the awarding body's own requirements before deciding whether anything further is needed.
Leave the submitted tenders as they are and add the statement to future documents only, since the process is complete and altering records now would be worse.
Ask Claude whether the documents would have been considered AI-assisted, and follow its judgement.
Remove the AI-assistance statement from the template, on the basis that the drafts were substantially written by staff.

questions.explanation: The organisation's disclosure requirement applies to documents **AI helped produce**, and 40 of these do. Adding it going forward is the minimum; the harder question is the two already submitted, and that depends on what the awarding body required — which the estates team is not in a position to guess. **Checking against the actual requirement** before deciding is the responsible order, and it also tells the organisation where its process has a gap.

whyWrong.B: Assuming no action is needed because the process is closed skips the check entirely. If disclosure was required, the position is better identified now than after an award is challenged.
whyWrong.C: Claude cannot determine what a third party's procurement rules require. Only the awarding body and the organisation's policy owners can say.
whyWrong.D: This treats the disclosure requirement as optional. How much staff edited a draft does not change what the tools produced it.

questions.mindset: A missed disclosure is fixed by finding out what was required, not by deciding it probably wasn't.

questions.scenario: Fernwood Legal's junior clerk has been asked by a partner to run a client questionnaire through Claude. The questionnaire asks for financial information about a very wealthy family. The firm's policy says: 'Where a client has not consented to AI use of their information, do not proceed.'
questions.stem: The partner believes the questionnaire is routine. The clerk has checked and there is no recorded consent. Which TWO actions are appropriate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Raise the policy point with the partner, and suggest either obtaining the client's consent or handling this particular questionnaire without Claude.
Remove the client's name from the questionnaire, since the information is about a family rather than an individual, and proceed.
Proceed, but only use the questionnaire to extract figures, not to draft any text from it.
Proceed, and note in the file that consent will be obtained before the next such questionnaire.
Proceed because the partner has instructed it, and record the instruction in the file.

questions.explanation: Two things are true at once. **A** is the right handling of the policy: the condition it names — consent — is not met, so either consent is obtained or the tool is not used for this questionnaire. **E** is also right, because when a client objects to their information being processed this way, that is their information to withhold; a partner's instruction cannot supply consent the client has not given. Both can be true: the instruction is followed *and* the material is not uploaded.

whyWrong.B: Removing a name does not remove the sensitivity. Financial position is identifiable personal information about a family, and other details in the questionnaire can identify them anyway.
whyWrong.C: Limiting what is produced does not change what was processed. The policy concerns the use of the information, not the format of the output.
whyWrong.D: Consent obtained later cannot retrospectively justify processing that already happened. This is consent-after-the-fact, which is not consent.

questions.mindset: A policy you route around today is a policy that does not exist next year. Surface the conflict while it is still cheap.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Care's HR team has drafted a guideline: 'Claude may be used to draft job descriptions, interview questions, offer letters and internal letters. It must not be used to shortlist, score, or make any recommendation about a candidate.'
questions.stem: A hiring manager wants to use Claude to compare interview notes against a scoring template and produce a shortlist of five from 60 applicants. Which TWO statements about the guideline are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Applying the scoring template to decide who progresses is a scoring decision about candidates, so it falls under what the guideline excludes.
It is permitted, because drafting the scoring template is permitted and applying it is simply the next step.
It is permitted, as long as the hiring manager reviews the shortlist and can override it.
Not permitted at all, so no hiring task of any kind may involve Claude.
The guideline leaves a gap, because it excludes scoring without saying who owns the judgement — closing that gap is what keeps it workable.

questions.explanation: **A**: the guideline draws its line by *where the judgement is made*, not by the name of the task. Drafting materials is permitted; using them to decide who progresses is the excluded step, and a human ratifying that ranking has not been given the criteria or the evidence to review it. **E** is the constructive observation — a guideline that excludes a step without saying who owns the judgement has left a gap, and closing it is how the guideline survives contact with a busy hiring manager.

whyWrong.B: The permission is bounded by the exclusion. "The next step after drafting" is still the excluded step, which is exactly why the wording names scoring and recommendation.
whyWrong.C: Review is what happens in the permitted tasks. For an excluded decision, the reviewer is asked to ratify a ranking they did not produce and are not equipped to audit.
whyWrong.D: This is the opposite over-correction. The guideline permits drafting, so blanket refusal would make a reasonable policy unusable and it would simply be ignored.

questions.mindset: Policies usually separate drafting from deciding. Find the line by locating the judgement, not the task name.

questions.scenario: Northgate Logistics is a haulage firm whose dispatch board is made up, historically, of people with similar backgrounds: mostly men, mostly white, mostly with driving rather than logistics-graduate experience. The board has asked to see how Claude scores candidates before it is used in shortlisting.
questions.stem: A pilot shows Claude scoring a female candidate and a candidate from an under-represented background lower than two comparably qualified candidates, and gives a plausible-sounding reason for each. What is the MOST responsible next step?

options.text: Do not use it to score, examine why the differences appear against a set of comparable cases, and if the pattern cannot be explained, do not proceed with scoring.
Use it, but ask Claude to include its reasoning for each score so the board can see whether the reasoning holds up.
Use it only for candidates from the groups the board has historically hired, where its judgements are least likely to be questioned.
Use it as one of several inputs alongside the board's own judgement, since averaging several judgements reduces the effect of any one being wrong.

questions.explanation: Discrimination in model outputs is a documented, measurable phenomenon, not a theoretical worry — which is why the test is to **look for the pattern on comparable cases** rather than to reason about whether it could exist. Asking for reasoning doesn't help, because a fabricated rationale sounds as convincing as a fabricated score. And averaging with human judgement doesn't neutralise a consistent bias; it can embed it while making it harder to see.

whyWrong.B: The reasoning is generated too, not retrieved. It will explain the score fluently whether or not the score reflects anything real.
whyWrong.C: Restricting use to the historically favoured group is discriminatory by design and indefensible if it ever surfaced.
whyWrong.D: Blending a systematically biased signal with human judgement does not cancel it, and it makes the influence of each input much harder to audit later.

questions.mindset: Test for discrimination on comparable cases. Never let a generated rationale stand in for evidence.

questions.scenario: Silverbrook Foods' marketing team uses Claude to draft the nutrition and sourcing claims on its packaging, and a claims officer checks each one against the lab report before print. The team has noticed that Claude's drafts are noticeably more favourable to the company than the evidence supports.
questions.stem: The claims officer has caught and corrected three overstated claims this quarter, and the team is under deadline pressure. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Treat it as a systematic pattern: tell Claude explicitly to write only what the evidence supports and to state when the evidence does not support a claim, and re-check the recent claims already published.
Strengthen the checking step so the claims officer verifies every factual claim against the lab report, and keep the drafting process as it is.
Keep the current process, since three corrected claims out of the whole quarter is a low enough error rate.
Ask Claude to include a footnote on each draft saying the claims are AI-drafted and pending verification.

questions.explanation: Three corrections in one quarter on a narrow claim type is not noise — it is a **systematic tendency** toward the company's interest, which is what you would expect from a drafting tool optimising for persuasive copy. Naming the tendency and correcting for it in the instructions addresses the cause; the human check addresses only the cases someone happens to catch. Claims already published also need reviewing, for the same reason the rate alone understates the problem.

whyWrong.B: This makes review the only defence against a systematic bias. It catches what the officer notices, and misses anything they do not — and public claims cannot be recalled.
whyWrong.C: Treating a rate as acceptable is exactly what makes this hard to spot. The relevant question is whether the errors share a direction, and here they do.
whyWrong.D: A footnote shifts responsibility onto the reader for claims the company chose to make, and public packaging claims are regulated.

questions.mindset: A repeated error in one direction is a pattern in the setup, not bad luck. Fix the setup and check what already went out.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Care runs a buddy scheme pairing new clinical staff with experienced colleagues. The programme manager uses Claude to write the invitations, the role descriptions for buddies, and the feedback forms.
questions.stem: A nurse points out that the draft invitations thank people for volunteering without ever explaining that the role involves night shifts and unsupervised cover on occasions. Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Make the expectations explicit and up front in the invitation, because informed volunteering depends on people understanding the commitment before they say yes.
Add the night-shift expectations to the buddy role description instead, so the invitation stays warm and the detail is documented in one place.
Keep the invitation as drafted but ask volunteers to confirm they have read the full role description before responding.
Ask colleagues who have done the role to describe what it actually involves, and use their words in the next draft.

questions.explanation: Ethical use of a drafting tool means the finished message actually serves the people it is written for. Someone agreeing to a role without knowing its demands is not genuinely consenting to it, however warm the invitation is. Putting the expectations **in the invitation itself** is the fix; this is the same logic behind disclosing that an assistant is AI — informed agreement has to happen before the yes, not after.

whyWrong.B: Burying the commitment in a separate document preserves the problem: the person saying yes still has not seen it. The invitation is where consent happens.
whyWrong.C: This is a procedural gesture. Asking for confirmation that a document was read is not the same as understanding what is in it.
whyWrong.D: Useful colour for improving the writing, but it improves tone rather than the substance — the omission was a material fact, not a lack of warmth.

questions.mindset: Consent has to happen before the yes, in the message where the yes happens.

questions.scenario: Rookwood Energy has used Claude to draft internal updates for two years. A new operations manager joins and finds the last six months of updates contain confident claims about pipeline and outage figures that she cannot trace to any source.
questions.stem: She asks her team how those figures were produced and gets three different answers. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Establish what was actually known at the time, and where a figure cannot be substantiated, correct the record — internally and, where it was communicated onward, in the same forum.
Note that the figures were AI-assisted, which discharges the team's obligation to be transparent about how they were produced.
Leave the historical updates in place, since correcting old updates is more disruptive than leaving them and only apply the fix going forward.
Ask Claude to re-check the six months of updates against current data and replace any figures it cannot support.

questions.explanation: When a figure has been repeated internally, correcting the record is part of the same obligation as not repeating it. Anything communicated onward to regulators, customers or partners carries the same need. The practical sequence is to establish what was actually known at the time — including where a number simply had no basis — and correct both the artefact and the audience. Going forward, the process change is separate and equally necessary.

whyWrong.B: Disclosing the mechanism addresses how, not whether. A figure nobody can source is inaccurate whether a person or a tool produced it.
whyWrong.C: This accepts that unsubstantiated figures remain part of the record indefinitely, which is how an organisation ends up with a reliability problem it can no longer assess.
whyWrong.D: Re-checking against *current* data is the wrong test for whether a historical claim was accurate when made, and it asks the same tool that produced the figures to audit itself.

questions.mindset: Untraceable figures have to be corrected in the same place they were repeated — disclosure of method is not a substitute.

questions.scenario: Halcyon Legal's paralegal team has used Claude to summarise police statements, client interviews and court bundles. The service operates on documents the firm receives, but its output is used in advice to clients who will never know it was involved.
questions.stem: The firm's managing partner is deciding whether to tell clients that AI is used in preparing advice. Which is the MOST defensible position?

options.text: Apply the firm's own disclosure rule consistently: disclose AI assistance in client-facing documents the policy names, and be able to explain the basis for each case, including where advice rests on a document the client has not seen.
Do not tell clients, because the client receives advice and not a description of how the advice was prepared.
Tell every client about every use, so that no client is treated differently from another.
Leave it to the individual lawyer who prepares each matter, provided they are satisfied the output is correct.

questions.explanation: The defensible position is consistency with a **stated rule plus a rationale**: apply the disclosure the firm has adopted, and be able to justify each case rather than decide case by case on instinct. Absolute disclosure is its own failure mode — a blanket statement that adds no useful information and erodes trust — while absolute silence leaves clients unable to assess how their material was handled. Leaving it to individual judgement produces exactly the inconsistency clients would notice if they compared.

whyWrong.B: Clients may reasonably want to know how documents containing sensitive personal material were processed. Whether a client sees the work is beside the point.
whyWrong.C: Uniformity is not the same as transparency. Telling every client everything, including uses that carry no meaningful information, satisfies nobody and trains people to ignore the disclosure.
whyWrong.D: This is the gap that produces inconsistent practice and the most damaging version of it: one lawyer deciding to disclose where another would not, with neither able to point to a rule.

questions.mindset: Have one stated rule and be able to justify each case. Both blanket silence and blanket disclosure fail.
